claims.text: The component architecture uses plasma-facing tungsten joined to a CuCrZr heat sink.
An intermediate layer is needed because tungsten and CuCrZr have incompatible operating-temperature ranges.
Current intermediate layers are tungsten-based high-entropy alloys.
Current tungsten-based HEA intermediate layers have limited heat-transfer efficiency.
Fusion-reactor plasma-facing components experience high temperatures, high heat fluxes, and intense irradiation.
Approximately 300–600 °C is a reactor-relevant operating range for the proposed intermediate layer.
Adding approximately 5 at.% Cu to a tungsten-based HEA will form uniformly dispersed nanoscale copper precipitates.
The nanoscale copper precipitates will form a percolating network within the HEA matrix.
A percolating copper-precipitate network will provide continuous heat-conduction paths through the alloy.
Copper has high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Fine copper precipitates can establish bridging networks that increase the alloy's effective heat transfer.
Keeping the copper content low will preserve the HEA matrix microstructure.
The retained HEA matrix will preserve high-temperature creep resistance and irradiation resistance.
Adding 5 at.% Cu will increase effective thermal conductivity relative to the undoped tungsten-based HEA.
The Cu-doped alloy will retain mechanical strength comparable to that of the undoped alloy under high-temperature, high-flux conditions.
The Cu-doped alloy will retain resistance to phase degradation comparable to that of the undoped alloy.
The predicted benefit will hold below approximately 700 °C.
Copper additions above approximately 10 at.% may cause deleterious phase segregation or loss of structural stability, while approximately 5 at.% is optimal.
